identity.name: GUJ NAR VAL FER & CHEM L

summary.oneLiner: GNFC delivered a strong Q4FY26 with PAT up 35% YoY to INR 797 Cr, driven by robust chemical realizations (TDI, AN) and technical grade urea substitution during war-induced logistics stress, though fertilizer margins remain suppressed pending government norm revisions. The near-term catalyst is the June-August commissioning of the coal-based power plant (CCPP) to arrest rising gas costs, while capex of INR 2,800 Cr in FY27 targets capacity expansion in Ammonium Nitrate and Ammonia.
summary.business: GNFC operates three principal business segments: a Fertilizer segment built around one of the largest single-stream Ammonia-Urea complexes, an Industrial Products (chemicals and petrochemicals) segment, and an Information Technology and Digital Services segment run through its (n)Code Solutions division. The fertilizer business sells urea and ammonium nitro phosphate to agricultural federations, cooperatives, agro-based industries, private distributors, institutional buyers and individual cultivators, and also trades bought-in fertilizers such as MoP, DAP, SSP and organic manure. The chemicals business is largely business-to-business, supplying bulk and intermediate chemicals to MSMEs, large industrial organisations, government bodies and public-sector enterprises as feedstock for specialty chemicals and end products.

Fertilizers: Neem Coated Urea (marketed under the Bharat brand, previously the Narmada brand)
Traded MoP, DAP, Ammonium Sulphate, SSP and City Compost
IT and Digital Services: GIS, smart cities, surveillance, system integration, cloud and hosting

currentContext.expansion: The single named growth project fully described in this bundle is the Ammonia Plant revamp. GNFC currently produces about 1,950 MTPD of Ammonia from both the fuel-oil and natural-gas route after the S-300 revamp, and plans to lift this to 2,100 MTPD by installing an Ammonia Make-up Gas Convertor Loop (AMUGL) in the existing Ammonia Synthesis Loop, which will also improve the reliability of that loop and add 50,000 MT of Ammonia per annum. An agreement has been signed with M/s. Topsoe, Denmark as technology licensor for the Basic Engineering Package, proprietary equipment and commissioning assistance; the project is on an EPC basis and is likely to be completed by the second quarter of FY 2027-28. A second project, a coal-based Captive Co-Generation Power Plant (CCPP) at Dahej, is introduced in this bundle but the text is cut off mid-sentence; what survives is that GNFC has set up a 100 MT/Hr gas-based boiler at the TDI-II Dahej complex for captive steam while power is sourced from the DGVCL grid, and that gas prices vary widely. Beyond these, the year's spending was largely reliability, energy-efficiency and debottlenecking work inside existing plants rather than new capacity: an NG preheater scheme implemented in April 2025 for energy savings with an H2 compressor installation for further energy optimisation in progress at the Ammonia Syngas plant; at the Urea plant a high-efficiency condensate pump and a high-capacity MP carbamate pump commissioned, the HP ammonia pump discharge isolation valve converted to a motor-operated valve, the new reactor foundation completed and a VFD for torque converter replacement under progress; replacement of the Ethyl Acetate plant reactor in December 2025; a Phase-I modification scheme for sustainable production at WNA-I plus cooling tower upgrades and partial completion of Phase-II, with VAM units commissioned during the year; permanent rectification of the WNA-II NOx exchanger leak during a scheduled shutdown; a control valve scheme in the ANMFS fire water system and mother liquor tank shell plate replacement at ANP; replacement of ion exchange resins at the DM plant; ongoing commissioning of diesel-driven firefighting pumps; and structural strengthening of the TDI plant Chlorine Scrubber initiated to enhance safety. Historically, the 50-year journey timeline reproduced in the report records the Ammonia-Urea complex (1982), entry into Aniline and TDI with Chematur, a 50,000 MTA Acetic Acid plant (1995), InfoTower Ahmedabad (1999), 21 MW of wind power in Kutch (2008), CNA-III and WNA-II (2011), an Ethyl Acetate plant and a 33 MW co-generation unit (2012), the Ammonia Syngas plant (2013), the Dahej TDI-II plant (2014), a 10 MW solar project at Charanka Solar Park, Patan (2020) and the 150 MTPD Concentrated Nitric Acid-IV plant (2023). NOTE ON COVERAGE: the Directors' Report text in this bundle is truncated in the middle of the CCPP paragraph, so any further on-going or new projects the company listed after that point are absent here and have not been supplied from any other source.

risks.risk: Import-substitute products exposed to fierce competition from dominant foreign suppliers
risks.note: Management's first stated risk and concern: most GNFC products are import substitutes, so pricing is set against dominant overseas producers rather than by domestic supply. This caps realisation in the chemical portfolio (TDI, acetic acid, formic acid, aniline) that now carries essentially all of the company's segment profit, and it means any dumping or capacity build-out abroad transmits straight to GNFC margins.

risks.risk: Raw material and feedstock concentration, purchased at import parity price from a narrow supplier base
risks.note: Key raw materials and feedstock are bought at import parity price and, in management's words, availability from a limited supplier base and at times almost a single pre-dominant source is a possible threat to profitable operations. GNFC mitigates with long/mid-term and annual contracts for coal, fuel oil, natural gas, rock phosphate, benzene, toluene and packaging, and is trying to broad-base the supplier list, but the structural dependence remains - the entire petroleum feed-stock requirement has come from a single counterparty since inception.

risks.risk: Fertilizer policy risk: NBS subsidy support may not track actual input costs, and energy norms are set without capital subsidy support
risks.note: Two of the four stated risks are policy risks. NBS support from time to time may not match actual input costs and hence may affect profitable operations; separately, energy norms for fertilizers being prescribed without capital subsidy support increases further strain on resources and is called a source of major risk. This shows up directly in results - higher energy norms in Urea are named as a driver of the fertilizer segment's wider loss.

risks.risk: Geopolitical disruption to gas and feedstock availability
risks.note: The Middle East conflict has disrupted global supply chains through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting international urea prices and constraining LNG availability, which management says may affect domestic urea production. This is already operational, not hypothetical: ASGP plant load is being restricted as per natural gas availability in view of the West Asia war crisis, two-gasifier operation was started in November 2025 because of it, TDI-II Dahej production was affected by natural gas supply constraints, and lower urea sales in March 2026 were attributed to limited feedstock supply for geo-political reasons.

risks.risk: Structural loss-making in the fertilizer segment, leaving profit concentrated in chemicals
risks.note: The fertilizer segment posted a segment loss again in FY 2025-26, slightly wider than the prior year on higher fixed cost, higher energy norms in Urea and lower volume, while the chemical segment carries essentially all of the company's segment result. Roughly a third of revenue therefore earns nothing, so group profitability is levered to a single segment's realisation and input-cost spread. India's import dependence - about 50% for DAP and nearly 100% for potash - and reliance on GoI subsidy, price control and import measures keep this segment structurally policy-dependent.

risks.risk: Monsoon, climate change and extreme weather
risks.note: IMD and Skymet have forecast a below-normal south-west monsoon for 2026 on El Nino conditions, with rainfall at 92-94% of the long period average, directly affecting Kharif fertilizer demand after an above-normal 2025 season. The BRSR separately identifies Climate Change Risk, noting exposure to water scarcity and the increasing frequency of extreme weather events with the potential to disrupt operations and adversely affect long-term business continuity, and warns that mitigation and resilience-building will require additional investment and raise costs.

The BRSR material-issues table flags that as a producer of fertilizers and chemical products GNFC's operations are inherently water-intensive and depend significantly on freshwater availability, exposing it to water scarcity from climatic variation and to reliance on local water sources, which may challenge operational continuity and the ability to maintain stable production levels. Increasing scarcity is expected to raise operating costs through greater reliance on alternative water sources. Mitigation cited includes 55 groundwater recharge wells in the green belt and a concrete storage reservoir.

risks.risk: Hazardous waste, environmental compliance and process safety at a large chemical complex
risks.note: Operations generate hazardous waste, exposing the company to regulatory compliance risk and higher operating costs, with practices governed by the Consolidated Consent & Authorization from the Gujarat Pollution Control Board and the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016; non-compliance may bring regulatory penalties and elevated disposal costs. Alongside this the BRSR flags inherent occupational health and safety risk, where workplace incidents or lapses may create compensation liabilities and higher insurance costs. The operational narrative corroborates the exposure - a synthesis gas compressor trip, repeated urea boiler tripping, an ethyl acetate reactor replaced for thickness reduction, a WNA-II NOx exchanger leak and structural strengthening of the TDI chlorine scrubber all occurred during the year.

The near-term catalyst is the June-August commissioning of the coal-based power plant (CCPP) to arrest rising gas costs, while capex of INR 2,800 Cr in FY27 targets capacity expansion in Ammonium Nitrate and Ammonia.
financial scorecard: Revenue: +7% YoY (Q4), +11% QoQ; EBITDA: Strong QoQ improvement (INR 300 Cr delta) driven by TDI, AN, TGU; PAT: INR 797 Cr (+35% YoY FY26), includes INR 80 Cr one-offs (FY26) vs INR 38 Cr (FY25); Order Book: N/A (Spot/Short-term contracts); Net Debt: Healthy balance sheet with internal accruals funding capex; One-offs: INR 30 Cr in Q4 (Insurance receipt INR 28 Cr + Freight escalation INR 15 Cr + Catalyst dust/penalty recoveries), partially offset by higher base.
guidance: Revenue Growth: Driven by volume ramp-up in AN/TDI; Margin: Expected improvement from H2FY27 post CCPP commissioning (saving INR 10-12 Cr/month); Order Inflow: Stable demand for AN (6-7% CAGR) and TGU; Capex: INR 2,800 Cr in FY27, additional undefined in FY28; Commissioning: CCPP by 3rd week June (sync) / 3rd week August (PGT); AN/Nitric Acid/Ammonia expansion by FY28.
order book & pipeline: Not applicable; Sales executed via variable price contracts (monthly/quarterly) linked to international benchmarks; Spot pricing dominates.
segment / subsidiary detail: Chemicals: Key profit driver; TDI, Ammonium Nitrate (+20% QoQ price), and Technical Grade Urea led Q4 EBITDA delta. Acetic Acid/Methanol volumes capped due to internal issues/high gas costs. Fertilizers: Urea segment loss-making due to unrevised fixed cost/energy norms; Complex fertilizers contributing at margin level. IT Division: Revenue +20%, Profit doubled to INR 35 Cr.
growth verticals / optionality: Ammonium Nitrate capacity expansion to capture import substitution (4-4.5 LMT current import); Coal-based chemical push by Govt boosts explosives demand; Potential urea policy changes (under evaluation); Downstream optimization (Ethyl Acetate) based on methanol/acetic acid arbitrage.
margins & cost dynamics: Pressure from high gas prices rendering methanol production unviable; Oil feedstock costs volatile (Hormuz tension); CCPP delay pushes cost savings to H2FY27; Aniline unviable standalone due to Chinese dumping and scale disadvantage.
capex / expansion: FY27: INR 2,800 Cr focused on Ammonia expansion, Nitric Acid, Ammonium Nitrate Melt, and CCPP; FY28: Further capex planned but quantum TBD; CCPP commissioning delayed to June-August FY27.
capital allocation: Dividend: 210% (INR 21/share), second highest in 50 years; Surplus cash parked in Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) with PSUs (e.g., GSFC) at ~7.25% yield; No buyback planned currently; Funding future capex via internal accruals.
risks & watch-items: Geopolitical: War impacting Hormuz logistics and raw material (Oil/Benzene/Toluene) availability/pricing; Regulatory: Delay in urea fixed cost/energy norm revision widening losses; Operational: CCPP further delays; Market: Chinese dumping in Aniline/TDI; Input Cost: Sustained high gas prices affecting methanol/acetic acid economics.
management quality / tone: Cautiously optimistic; Emphasized resilience during war (TGU supply); Transparent on CCPP delays and fertilizer segment headwinds; Disciplined on capital allocation (high dividend, PSU ICDs); Non-committal on aniline expansion due to structural unviability.
non-obvious takeaways: Management revealed that 45% of Captive Nitrobenzene (CNA) production is sold externally (rubber chemical sector), not just captive; The 'loans and advances' spike to INR 2,400 Cr is strategic parking in PSU ICDs for yield (7.25%) rather than operational working capital bloating; TDI operating rate capped at ~80% due to global technical complexity, not demand constraints.
challenges → beneficiaries & losers:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| War-induced diesel exhaust fluid shortage requiring urgent TGU supply | Indian Oil Corp Ltd | beneficiary | Med | GNFC doubled TGU production to support BS6 logistics, stabilizing downstream fuel distribution for OMCs. |
| Rising coal mining targets requiring domestic explosives feedstock | Coal India Ltd | beneficiary | High | Govt push for coal-based chemicals and mining expansion directly benefits GNFC's Ammonium Nitrate capacity addition, reducing import dependence for Coal India's explosives needs. |
| High gas prices making methanol production unviable | GAIL India Ltd | loser | Low | While GNFC cuts methanol output, the root cause is high gas pricing which pressures GAIL's marketing margins if passed through, though GNFC's pivot to buying methanol may support GAIL's trading volumes. |

themes.title: Industrial gases, chlor-alkali & commodity chemicals
themes.need: A capacity-led commodity-chemical and industrial-gas cycle underpins the basic-materials chain - ELLEN on air-separation/industrial gases; EPIGRAL/CHEMPLASTS/DCW/DCMSHRIRAM/GHCL/TATACHEM/GNFC on chlor-alkali, soda-ash and vinyls; LORDSCHLO on caustic; CHEMBONDCH on water-treatment chemicals. Pricing/utilization and energy costs are the near-term swing factors.
themes.driver: Caustic/soda-ash price recovery; utilization ramp on new capacity; energy-cost relief.

themes.title: Fertilizer subsidy & nutrient-policy cycle
themes.need: Fertilizer makers are driven by NBS/urea subsidy policy, gas-pooling and nutrient pricing rather than the crop-protection volume/molecule-launch recovery. Q1FY27's supply-side read comes from MBAPL: revenue roughly flat at INR 416cr with EBITDA +16% and PAT +17% purely on cheap March-bought raw material that management said is now EXHAUSTED, with utilisation only ~43-45% because of raw-material availability rather than demand - SSP sales were +28% and NPK +33% YoY against production down 7%/28%. Its Dhule (Maharashtra) integrated complex commissions +3,30,000 MTPA DAP-NPK plus 99,000 MTPA phosphoric acid in Oct-2026 and a second phase in Oct-2027, framed as a >50% turnover jump toward ~INR 3,500cr revenue and 15.6 lakh MT capacity by FY28; Egypt/Jordan rock-phosphate sourcing (non-Hormuz) insulated it relative to import-dependent peers. Subsidy clarity and gas costs still set the near-term margin.
themes.driver: NBS/urea subsidy policy (the Oct-Mar rate revision), gas-pooling and nutrient pricing; MBAPL's Oct-2026 Dhule commissioning and the utilisation ramp toward ~90%; kharif demand pull-through after a delayed monsoon.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: GNFC operates three principal business segments: a Fertilizer segment built around one of the largest single-stream Ammonia-Urea complexes, an Industrial Products (chemicals and petrochemicals) segment, and an Information Technology and Digital Services segment run through its (n)Code Solutions division. The fertilizer business sells urea and ammonium nitro phosphate to agricultural federations, cooperatives, agro-based industries, private distributors, institutional buyers and individual cultivators, and also trades bought-in fertilizers such as MoP, DAP, SSP and organic manure. The chemicals business is largely business-to-business, supplying bulk and intermediate chemicals to MSMEs, large industrial organisations, government bodies and public-sector enterprises as feedstock for specialty chemicals and end products.

group_structure.title: Group structure (profile)
group_structure.body:
- Gujarat Green Revolution Company Limited — associate: Associate company, 46.87% of shares held by the listed entity per BRSR Section A item 23; the BRSR records that it does not participate in the Business Responsibility initiatives of the listed entity. Appears in the related-party note as an Associate from which GNFC receives dividend.
- Gujarat State Fertilizers & Chemicals Limited — related party: Promoter company; related-party transactions comprise purchase of goods and services by GNFC and dividend paid to it.
- Gujarat State Investments Ltd. — related party: Promoter company; related-party transaction is dividend paid to it.
- Narmadanagar Rural Development Society — related party: Classified as 'Other related party'; transactions are towards CSR activities.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body: Chemicals: Key profit driver; TDI, Ammonium Nitrate (+20% QoQ price), and Technical Grade Urea led Q4 EBITDA delta. Acetic Acid/Methanol volumes capped due to internal issues/high gas costs. Fertilizers: Urea segment loss-making due to unrevised fixed cost/energy norms; Complex fertilizers contributing at margin level. IT Division: Revenue +20%, Profit doubled to INR 35 Cr.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Fertilizers:** Neem Coated Urea (marketed under the Bharat brand, previously the Narmada brand), Ammonium Nitro Phosphate (20-20-0), Fermented Organic Manure (FOM), Traded MoP, DAP, Ammonium Sulphate, SSP and City Compost
- **Industrial Products / Chemicals:** Toluene Di-Isocyanate (TDI), Acetic Acid, Formic Acid, Methyl Formate, Technical Grade Urea (TGU), Aniline, Concentrated Nitric Acid, Weak Nitric Acid, Ethyl Acetate, Methanol, AN Melt / Ammonium Nitrate, Ammonia, CATSOL catalyst
- **Consumer / neem-based:** Neo Neem Soap, Hand Wash
- **IT and Digital Services:** (n)Code Solutions, (n)Procure e-procurement, e-Governance services, PKI and digital signatures, GIS, smart cities, surveillance, system integration, cloud and hosting

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: Not applicable; Sales executed via variable price contracts (monthly/quarterly) linked to international benchmarks; Spot pricing dominates.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue Growth: Driven by volume ramp-up in AN/TDI; Margin: Expected improvement from H2FY27 post CCPP commissioning (saving INR 10-12 Cr/month); Order Inflow: Stable demand for AN (6-7% CAGR) and TGU; Capex: INR 2,800 Cr in FY27, additional undefined in FY28; Commissioning: CCPP by 3rd week June (sync) / 3rd week August (PGT); AN/Nitric Acid/Ammonia expansion by FY28.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: Ammonium Nitrate capacity expansion to capture import substitution (4-4.5 LMT current import); Coal-based chemical push by Govt boosts explosives demand; Potential urea policy changes (under evaluation); Downstream optimization (Ethyl Acetate) based on methanol/acetic acid arbitrage.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian chemical market estimated at approximately $155-165 billion is expected to reach $230-255 billion by 2030, implying a CAGR of 8-9%, a trajectory management expects to outpace overall GDP growth
- Chemical demand support expected from traditional GDP-linked sectors (consumer goods, packaging, textiles, automotive, construction) plus emerging areas such as electric vehicles, renewable energy and semiconductors
- An India supply-demand gap of $20 billion to $30 billion, plus higher exports, is identified as an accelerant for India-based chemical companies willing to align capital to demand drivers
- Performance is diverging within the chemical industry, with specialty and niche chemicals showing greater resilience than commoditized products - framed as an inflection point for reassessing capital allocation and positioning
- Fertilizer industry described as structurally resilient, supported by rising food demand, limited arable land and increasing crop intensity, with India showing steady consumption growth driven by policy support and agricultural dependence
- FY26 demand backdrop was favourable: the 2025 south-west monsoon delivered 108% of Long Period Average rainfall, Kharif acreage reached 1121 lakh hectare (2% above normal) and Rabi acreage 677 lakh hectare (6% above normal); in GNFC's own operating states Kharif coverage was 123% and Rabi 106% of normal
- Total food grain production for 2025-26 estimated at 348.65 million tonnes against 330.9 MT in 2024-25 (second advance estimates)
- MSPs for most Kharif and Rabi crops rose 2% to 10% over the previous year, though management notes the MSP impact was almost nil on 12 of the 17 crops over the past three years
- NBS rates rose materially year on year - Rabi 2025-26 versus Rabi 2024-25 up 36% for DAP, 23% for ANP and 45% for SSP - and GoI has fixed DAP MRP at Rs 1,350 per bag with 'other costs' reimbursement of Rs 3,500 pmt continued for Kharif-26
- International fertilizer and input prices moved against the company on most lines between Mar'25 and Mar'26 (urea +20%, ammonia +24%, MOP +23%, phosphoric acid +22%), while natural gas fell 30%
- Chemical segment margin lever in FY26 came from lower input cost, higher realisation, penalty income received due to delay in operation of the CCPP plant, and lower fixed cost, partially offset by lower volume
- Fertilizer segment remained loss-making, with higher fixed cost, higher energy norms in Urea and lower volume as the stated drags
- (n)Code Solutions growth driven by new project wins in the e-Governance vertical and continued growth in (n)procure services, with fixed costs largely stable
- MDA of Rs 1,500 per MT on sales of Fermented Organic Manure is going to conclude this year, with its impact under evaluation by NITI Aayog - a policy watch-item for the FOM push
- Revenue comparability caveat: management notes FY 2025-26 revenue from operations is not comparable because of the annual turnaround at Bharuch Complex this year versus at Dahej Complex in FY 2024-25
- No conventional order book is disclosed in this bundle - GNFC sells commodity fertilizers and chemicals rather than against an order backlog
- The nearest pipeline disclosure is for the IT division: (n)Code Solutions cites new project wins in the e-Governance vertical, particularly in the education sector for various Government of Gujarat departments covering recruitment processes and allied services, and the onboarding of MSME Commissioner and Statue of Unity (SOU) as a new client

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Pressure from high gas prices rendering methanol production unviable; Oil feedstock costs volatile (Hormuz tension); CCPP delay pushes cost savings to H2FY27; Aniline unviable standalone due to Chinese dumping and scale disadvantage.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Dividend: 210% (INR 21/share), second highest in 50 years; Surplus cash parked in Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) with PSUs (e.g., GSFC) at ~7.25% yield; No buyback planned currently; Funding future capex via internal accruals.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The single named growth project fully described in this bundle is the Ammonia Plant revamp. GNFC currently produces about 1,950 MTPD of Ammonia from both the fuel-oil and natural-gas route after the S-300 revamp, and plans to lift this to 2,100 MTPD by installing an Ammonia Make-up Gas Convertor Loop (AMUGL) in the existing Ammonia Synthesis Loop, which will also improve the reliability of that loop and add 50,000 MT of Ammonia per annum. An agreement has been signed with M/s. Topsoe, Denmark as technology licensor for the Basic Engineering Package, proprietary equipment and commissioning assistance; the project is on an EPC basis and is likely to be completed by the second quarter of FY 2027-28. A second project, a coal-based Captive Co-Generation Power Plant (CCPP) at Dahej, is introduced in this bundle but the text is cut off mid-sentence; what survives is that GNFC has set up a 100 MT/Hr gas-based boiler at the TDI-II Dahej complex for captive steam while power is sourced from the DGVCL grid, and that gas prices vary widely. Beyond these, the year's spending was largely reliability, energy-efficiency and debottlenecking work inside existing plants rather than new capacity: an NG preheater scheme implemented in April 2025 for energy savings with an H2 compressor installation for further energy optimisation in progress at the Ammonia Syngas plant; at the Urea plant a high-efficiency condensate pump and a high-capacity MP carbamate pump commissioned, the HP ammonia pump discharge isolation valve converted to a motor-operated valve, the new reactor foundation completed and a VFD for torque converter replacement under progress; replacement of the Ethyl Acetate plant reactor in December 2025; a Phase-I modification scheme for sustainable production at WNA-I plus cooling tower upgrades and partial completion of Phase-II, with VAM units commissioned during the year; permanent rectification of the WNA-II NOx exchanger leak during a scheduled shutdown; a control valve scheme in the ANMFS fire water system and mother liquor tank shell plate replacement at ANP; replacement of ion exchange resins at the DM plant; ongoing commissioning of diesel-driven firefighting pumps; and structural strengthening of the TDI plant Chlorine Scrubber initiated to enhance safety. Historically, the 50-year journey timeline reproduced in the report records the Ammonia-Urea complex (1982), entry into Aniline and TDI with Chematur, a 50,000 MTA Acetic Acid plant (1995), InfoTower Ahmedabad (1999), 21 MW of wind power in Kutch (2008), CNA-III and WNA-II (2011), an Ethyl Acetate plant and a 33 MW co-generation unit (2012), the Ammonia Syngas plant (2013), the Dahej TDI-II plant (2014), a 10 MW solar project at Charanka Solar Park, Patan (2020) and the 150 MTPD Concentrated Nitric Acid-IV plant (2023). NOTE ON COVERAGE: the Directors' Report text in this bundle is truncated in the middle of the CCPP paragraph, so any further on-going or new projects the company listed after that point are absent here and have not been supplied from any other source.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Cautiously optimistic; Emphasized resilience during war (TGU supply); Transparent on CCPP delays and fertilizer segment headwinds; Disciplined on capital allocation (high dividend, PSU ICDs); Non-committal on aniline expansion due to structural unviability.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Sole or near-sole domestic supply position: the BRSR states GNFC is the only producer of Acetic Acid and Formic Acid in India, has the largest single-stream Aniline plant in India, and is the only manufacturer of Toluene Di-Isocyanate in Southeast Asia and the Indian Sub-Continent
- Import-substitution positioning - the Corporate Overview describes the Chemicals Business as advancing India goals of self-reliance and import substitution through a diversified portfolio serving critical industries
- Structurally secured feedstock: IOCL has met the entire petroleum feed-stock requirement (HSFO/LSHS-P/FOHV) since inception, and the supply agreement is to be extended till 30-4-2031
- Long/mid-term and annual contracts for most critical raw materials - coal, oil, natural gas, rock phosphate, benzene, toluene and packaging materials - supporting continuous production
- Sustained debottlenecking and revamping has lifted output above rated capacity across many plants; 30 new records were established in FY 2025-26, of which 20 in production and 10 in filling/dispatch/sales
- Captive energy assets - a co-generation power and steam unit, 21 MW wind in Kutch, 10 MW solar at Charanka and a gas-based captive boiler at Dahej
- Own retail distribution to farmers through Narmada Khedut Sahay Kendras (NKSKs), COCO-model retail outlets offering bulk and non-bulk agri-inputs plus advisory services
- Diversification across fertilizers, chemicals and IT services, with the IT division embedded in Government of Gujarat procurement through (n)Procure, which is extended to all Government of Gujarat departments

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Geopolitical: War impacting Hormuz logistics and raw material (Oil/Benzene/Toluene) availability/pricing; Regulatory: Delay in urea fixed cost/energy norm revision widening losses; Operational: CCPP further delays; Market: Chinese dumping in Aniline/TDI; Input Cost: Sustained high gas prices affecting methanol/acetic acid economics.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Management revealed that 45% of Captive Nitrobenzene (CNA) production is sold externally (rubber chemical sector), not just captive; The 'loans and advances' spike to INR 2,400 Cr is strategic parking in PSU ICDs for yield (7.25%) rather than operational working capital bloating; TDI operating rate capped at ~80% due to global technical complexity, not demand constraints.

challenges.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers
challenges.body:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| War-induced diesel exhaust fluid shortage requiring urgent TGU supply | Indian Oil Corp Ltd | beneficiary | Med | GNFC doubled TGU production to support BS6 logistics, stabilizing downstream fuel distribution for OMCs. |
| Rising coal mining targets requiring domestic explosives feedstock | Coal India Ltd | beneficiary | High | Govt push for coal-based chemicals and mining expansion directly benefits GNFC's Ammonium Nitrate capacity addition, reducing import dependence for Coal India's explosives needs. |
| High gas prices making methanol production unviable | GAIL India Ltd | loser | Low | While GNFC cuts methanol output, the root cause is high gas pricing which pressures GAIL's marketing margins if passed through, though GNFC's pivot to buying methanol may support GAIL's trading volumes. |

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Regulation — NCU energy norm] DoF notification dated 30-6-26 fixes the New Energy Norm for Neem Coated Urea at 6.37 Gcal PMT from 1-4-25 to 31-3-28, against the earlier norm of 6.20 Gcal PMT. "As per preliminary assessment, there will be positive financial impact of approximately Rs 61 crores for Apr-25 to Jun-26 which will be accounted for in Q-2-FY-26-27 after detailed examination."
- [Regulation — pending] "The revision in fixed cost for NCU is being pursued with the Government at industry level."
- [Geopolitics] "Company continues to closely monitor geopolitical developments and are proactively taking necessary actions to safeguard interest of all Stakeholders"; the deck attributes lower chemical volumes and segment-result pressure to geopolitical challenges.
- [Disclosure policy] The cautionary slide states: "As a matter of policy, we do not provide any forecast about the future business situation" and "We do not comment or give guidance on future results or business outlook" — so the deck carries no guidance.
- [Other comprehensive income] Change in OCI is attributed to "change in the fair market value of both quoted and unquoted investments as well as actuarial assumptions of employee benefit obligations".
